extracted.intended_audience: aspiring cozy-mystery novelists / fiction writers interested in the cozy subgenre
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, plotting, characterizing, and publishing a cozy mystery novel (and building it into a series) that fits genre expectations and delights readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre content & violence restrictions (PG/PG-13 suitability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The crime is not exceedingly cruel. There’s no torture, sexual crimes, or violence against children or animals. Murder rarely happens on the page and, when it does, there’s little to no blood. Cozy mystery is rated PG or PG-13: no strong language or graphic violence; if there’s sex it happens off page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use non-graphic means (poison is a popular go-to). Avoid sexual violence, child/animal abuse, explicit gore, and strong language. Keep the overall content family-friendly to align with reader expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and emotional texture (lightheartedness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cozy mysteries are lighthearted — they contain tension and suspense but the humor is softer than in hardboiled or gritty crime fiction, and the world feels comforting despite the crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for an inviting, gently humorous tone; avoid cynical snipes and bleak nihilism. Maintain a sense of comfort and escapism even as stakes rise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and economy (word-count expectations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cozies are usually on the shorter end; cozy mystery books are sometimes as short as 50,000 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t pad unnecessarily; favor brisk pacing and focused storytelling appropriate to a shorter novel length common in the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting must feel idyllic, safe, and charming
rubrics_metrics.description: Settings are unreasonably charming (idyllic small towns, ski lodges, boutique hotels) and the world of the story should seem safe and comforting even when crime occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create immersive, attractive locales readers want to inhabit. Use setting shifts (e.g., quiet streets feeling ominous at night) to change atmosphere for scenes. Show rather than tell the charm and safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cozy tropes and recurring motifs
rubrics_metrics.description: Beloved genre tropes include the idyllic small town (Cabot Cove syndrome), amateur sleuths with quaint careers or hobbies (baking, knitting, floral design), and charming motifs woven through the story (e.g., baking puns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage tropes and motifs to meet reader expectations and to give the series a distinct flavor—use the protagonist’s interests as running motifs and to plausibly tie into clues and plot events. Be mindful of trope fatigue but play to what readers love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot structure and pacing (Fichtean curve recommended)
rubrics_metrics.description: There’s no required structure, but the Fichtean curve is recommended for its tension-building simplicity. A good cozy introduces the crime early, establishes stakes, continually raises stakes, allows the sleuth to make wrong turns, and culminates in a confrontation with the perpetrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get to the crime quickly (discovery of the body or early inciting incident). Establish what’s at stake for the protagonist. Raise suspense and urgency steadily. Permit the detective to pursue false leads to maintain tension. Build to a climax where the sleuth confronts the villain (dramatic confrontation preferred over simply presenting evidence to police).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clues, red herrings, and twist construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Drop real clues so the ending is supported; throw red herrings to mislead readers; craft twists by inviting plausible assumptions and then subverting them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure twist reveals are fair — the supporting details must exist earlier (subtle, sparse, but present). Use red herrings to complicate the reader’s and sleuth’s path without cheating. Avoid twists that feel unearned or that betray the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist (detective) characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: The detective is typically a relatable, ordinary-person protagonist (often an amateur) whose life feels familiar outside the murder business. Establish credibility and a believable sleuthing 'superpower.' Cozy protagonists often have flat or positive arcs within a single book but can develop across a series; they should still face personal challenges and some internal conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the sleuth likable, competent in a way tied to their life/skills, and emotionally accessible. Give them a plausible reason to investigate. Use modest internal stakes rather than heavy transformational arcs in a single title, reserving deeper change for series development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetrator motive and backstory
rubrics_metrics.description: Perps should have a clear and compelling motive (greed, secrecy, jealousy are good options). Avoid extremely dark, psychologically complex, or abusive backstories typical of grittier crime fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep motives understandable and grounded in everyday human failings rather than depravity or severe mental illness. Make motive believable and tied into the victim’s and suspects’ histories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Victim construction and usefulness to plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Victims are almost always unlikeable in cozies. Because dead characters can only exist as backstory, the victim should have a developed history that gives the sleuth threads to follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a full backstory for the victim that explains relationships, grudges, secrets, and potential motives among other characters. An unlikeable victim makes it easier to plausibly populate a roster of suspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspect ensemble and secret-keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspects should have backstories entwined with the victim and at least a few hidden secrets so that innocent characters can convincingly appear guilty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft interpersonal ties between suspects and victim. Plant believable secrets that raise suspicion and can be revealed over the investigation to shift suspicion and sustain mystery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key side characters and law enforcement roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary cast should include professional law enforcement (who may love or hate collaborating with the amateur sleuth), family and friends who create calm or conflict, and antagonists who obstruct the investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use side characters to enrich the world, add obstacles or support, and provide alternate perspectives. Balance police competence and reluctance to collaborate for dramatic friction without undercutting plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series planning: continuity, freshness, and long arcs
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan for continuity (consistent details across books), keep characters and settings fresh but don’t transform the world too much, and consider adding a series-wide plot (cold case, returning perp) that remains secondary to each book’s primary storyline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain meticulous notes about recurring details (use tools like Dabble). Allow secondary characters to change (babies, new jobs) to keep things alive while preserving core series elements. Weave a slow-burning series arc that rewards repeat readers but doesn’t prevent new readers from enjoying a single book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beta readers, revision, and publishing routes
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sending to gatekeepers or releasing, share your novel with beta readers to get reader-perspective notes on twists and atmosphere. Common publishing routes include traditional and self-publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use beta reader feedback to verify whether twists land, whether suspense and atmosphere work, and whether the setting is immersive. Choose publishing route based on goals; beta feedback is crucial either way. Tools and templates (e.g., Dabble’s mystery template) can aid organization and revision.
